newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: DEADLINE FOR EXTORTIONISTS PASSES
The deadline for the Arnotts extortionists passed at midnight and a decision is expected to be made today on whether Arnotts biscuits can return to supermarket shelves.
Eleven days ago, all Arnotts stock was pulled off shelves in Queensland and New South Wales after extortionists threatened to poison biscuits and put them back on shelves.
Police are expected to make an announcement later today on whether the threat to public safety is officially over.
About three weeks ago, letters and biscuits laced with pesticide were sent to authorities demanding New South Wales detectives take lie dectector tests about their evidence in a 1993 murder trail.
Last week, police issued an ultimatum, they'd consider the threat over if those responsible failed to contact them by midnight last night.
CHINA MOURNS LOSS OF LEADER AT FUNERAL TODAY
China will virtually come to a standstill for 90 minutes today during the funeral service of paramount leader Deng Xiaping.
On this last day of official mourning, ships, trains, and factories have been ordered to blow horns and whistles for three minutes.
All work units have been ordered to stop work and tune into the live telecast of the service.
The funeral ceremony will be held at the Great Hall of the people.
Yesterday Chinese television, for the first time, showed pictures of Xiaping's body lying in a glass coffin.
EX-CYCLONE ITA CAUSING FLOODING
In north Queensland, Tropical Cyclone Ita crossed the coast south east of Townsville last night bringing with it heavy rain and gale force winds.
The system turned into a rain depression overnight.
Floodwaters have cut the Bruce Highway at Guthalungra halfway between Ayr and Bowen, and coastal rivers between Townsville and Mackay are flooding.
Last night wind and lightning near Ayr brought down two power lines affecting power to some residents.
The weather system is weakening near Charters Towers and heading south west.
STRIKE PLANNED UNLESS PAY BETTER OFFER AT NSW UNI
The National Tertiary Education Union will be looking for an improved salary offer from the University of New South Wales when enterprise bargaining talks resume today.
Academics at the university plan to strike next week on Monday and Tuesday, the first two days of the new academic year, unless the offer is improved.
The university is one of the last to resolve the union's request for improved salaries for staff, which has secured increases of 11- to 12-percent over two years at other institutions.
SEARCH FOR SEWAGE LINK IN HEPATITIS A OUTBREAK
Sewage discharges into Wallis Lake on the mid north coast are being investigated as the link to the Hepatitis A outbreak.
Health authorities announced yesterday that a 77-year-old man had died of the illness, he was one of 300 Hepatitis A cases reported in the state in the past five weeks.
Wallis Lake oysters have also been held responsible for illness among residents of three other states.
Investigations continue into whether sewage from septic tanks in the town of Nabiac and a local caravan park have contaminated Wallis Lake.
AUSTRALIA WOULD GET FALLOUT FROM NUCLEAR PROGRAM: WARNING
The Free East Timor group says Darwin will be in the firing line of any accident if a nuclear reactor is built on the earthquake-prone island of Java
Rob Wesley-Smith, from Australians for a Free East Timor, told a uranium conference in Darwin that monsoonal weather would bring the radioactive fallout to northern Australia.
He says Indonesia should find more efficient ways to use energy or look to alternative energy sources rather than move to nuclear power.
An official from the Indonesian Atomic Energy Agency BATAN, yesterday told the conference nuclear power was the most logical way of meeting future energy demand.
UNION DEFENDS USE OF BULL-BARS IN THE BUSH
The Cattlemen's Union says calls for a national ban on bull-bars are an over-reaction.
The Pedestrian Council of Australia has called for a ban claiming bull-bars increase the likelihood of death and injury to pedestrians, drivers and passengers in motor vehicle accidents.
But Cattlemen's Union executive director Ruth Wade say the union believes they are effective at protecting people and vehicles from collisions with animals.
He says more research is needed before any blanket ban of bull-bars across Australia is considered.
